blocks.text: A 1.4 tonne car travelling at motorway speed carries more than half a megajoule of kinetic energy, and every joule of it must leave the car through the brakes as heat within a few seconds. Brake design is about two things: how much friction torque can be generated by a given pedal force, and where the heat goes.

blocks.markdown: A brake converts kinetic energy into heat by friction. In a **drum brake** shoes press outwards on the inside of a rotating drum; in a **disc brake** pads clamp the sides of a rotating disc. The retarding torque is friction force times radius, $T=\mu Nr$, where $\mu$ is the coefficient of friction between lining and drum (typically 0.3 to 0.4 for organic linings on cast iron, a representative value), $N$ is the normal force between shoe and drum and $r$ the drum radius. The design problem is to find $N$ from the actuating force, and to find the energy to be absorbed.

blocks.title: Self-energising brake
blocks.text: In a self-energising shoe the friction force on the shoe, generated by the rotating drum, produces a moment about the shoe pivot that helps to press the shoe on the drum. The actuating force then produces a larger normal force, and so a larger braking torque, than it would without the friction effect. When the rotation is reversed the same friction force opposes the actuating force and the shoe is de-energising.

blocks.markdown: **Short-shoe analysis.** If the shoe is short compared with the drum, the contact pressure can be replaced by one normal force $N$ at one point and a friction force $\mu N$ tangent to the drum. The shoe lever is hinged at a pin $O$. Define the distances perpendicular from the pin to the lines of action of the forces: $a$ for the actuating force $F$, $b$ for the normal force $N$ and $c$ for the friction force $\mu N$. Taking moments about the pin gives the normal force, with the upper sign when friction helps (self-energising) and the lower sign when friction opposes (de-energising).

blocks.latex: F\,a=N\,(b\mp\mu c)\ \Rightarrow\ N=\frac{Fa}{b\mp\mu c},\qquad T=\mu N r=\frac{\mu F a\,r}{b\mp\mu c}
blocks.caption: Short-shoe drum brake: braking torque for self-energising (minus sign) and de-energising (plus sign) rotation

blocks.title: Braking torque in both directions
blocks.prompt: A short shoe is operated by a force $F=400$ N acting at perpendicular distance $a=300$ mm from the pin. The perpendicular distances from the pin to the normal and friction forces are $b=150$ mm and $c=200$ mm, the drum radius is $r=250$ mm and $\mu=0.3$. Find the braking torque when the shoe is self-energising and when it is de-energising, and the condition for self-locking.

steps.text: Self-energising: the denominator is reduced by the friction moment.
Ratio of the two torques, and the self-locking condition: the denominator $b-\mu c$ becomes zero (the brake grabs with no actuating force) when $\mu=b/c=0.75$.

blocks.answer: The braking torque is 100 N m self-energising and 43 N m de-energising, a ratio of 2.3. The brake would self-lock if $\mu\geq0.75$.

rows: Brake torque per unit pedal force
Lower; needs a servo or hydraulics
High: $T\propto\mu/(b-\mu c)$, so fade or a wet lining changes torque strongly
Rear axle, parking brake, heavy duty
Front axle and most modern vehicles
blocks.caption: Drum and disc brakes compared

blocks.markdown: **Energy to be dissipated.** In a single stop the brake must absorb the kinetic energy that the rotating or translating system has. For a rotating inertia $I$ (kg m$^2$) at angular speed $\omega$ (rad/s) the energy is $\tfrac12I\omega^2$. For a vehicle of mass $m$ at speed $v$ it is $\tfrac12mv^2$, plus any rotational inertia, and potential energy if braking on a downhill gradient. With a constant braking torque $T$ the stopping time is $t=I\omega/T$, and the mean power absorbed is $E/t$, which is $T\omega/2$.

blocks.caption: Energy absorbed in a stop, stopping time at constant torque and mean power (SI)

blocks.title: Stopping a rotating flywheel
blocks.prompt: A flywheel of inertia $I=4.5$ kg m$^2$ rotates at 1200 rev/min and is stopped by a brake with a constant torque of 100 N m. Find the energy absorbed, the stopping time and the mean braking power.
blocks.answer: The brake absorbs 35.5 kJ in 5.65 s, at a mean power of 6.28 kW (peak power at the start is twice that).

blocks.markdown: **Temperature rise of a disc.** In a single short stop there is no time for much heat to escape, so as a first estimate all of the energy that the disc absorbs raises its temperature uniformly. If the disc has mass $m_d$ and specific heat $c_p$ (cast iron or steel: about 450 to 500 J/(kg K), typical), the rise is $\Delta T=E_d/(m_dc_p)$. The share of the energy taken by a given disc depends on the brake-force distribution between front and rear, typically 60 to 70 per cent on the front axle in a passenger car. The calculation ignores cooling, so it is an upper bound for one stop, and repeated stops need a heat-transfer analysis.

blocks.latex: \Delta T=\frac{E_d}{m_d\,c_p},\qquad E_d=\frac{\text{(share of axle)}\times E}{\text{number of discs on that axle}}
blocks.caption: Adiabatic single-stop temperature rise of a brake disc

blocks.title: Disc temperature rise in a single stop
blocks.prompt: A 1400 kg car brakes from 100 km/h to rest. 70 per cent of the braking energy goes to the front axle, which has two identical discs of mass 7.5 kg each with $c_p=500$ J/(kg K). Estimate the temperature rise of one front disc, ignoring cooling and rotational inertia.

steps.text: Speed in SI units and kinetic energy.
Energy per front disc, a share of 70 per cent split between two discs.

blocks.answer: The kinetic energy is 540 kJ, each front disc absorbs about 189 kJ and its temperature rises by about 50 K in the stop.

blocks.title: Repeated stops and fade
blocks.text: A rise of 50 K from a single stop is modest, but repeated stops (for example descending a long hill) give a cumulative rise because the disc cannot cool in time. High temperatures lower the friction coefficient (fade) and may crack the disc, so brakes are also designed on the basis of continuous power dissipation and cooling.

points: Short-shoe drum brake: $T=\mu Fa\,r/(b\mp\mu c)$, with the minus sign for the self-energising direction; self-locking occurs when $\mu\ge b/c$.
Self-energising brakes give much larger torque but are sensitive to changes in $\mu$, while disc brakes give $T\propto\mu$ and a more stable braking effect.
The energy absorbed in a stop is $\tfrac12I\omega^2$ or $\tfrac12mv^2$ (and potential energy if downhill); at constant torque the stopping time is $I\omega/T$.
Single-stop disc temperature rise is $\Delta T=E_d/(m_dc_p)$, an upper bound that ignores cooling.

questions.stem: What is meant by a self-energising drum brake shoe?

options.text: The friction force on the shoe produces a moment about its pivot that helps to press the shoe against the drum
The shoe presses itself on the drum without any actuating force
The shoe generates electricity during braking
The shoe cools itself by self-ventilation

questions.correctOptionText: The friction force on the shoe produces a moment about its pivot that helps to press the shoe against the drum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: friction assists the actuating force, raising the normal force and braking torque.
distractorRationale.b: That describes self-locking, a limiting case.
distractorRationale.c: That is regenerative braking, a different concept.

questions.explanation: In the self-energising direction the friction moment about the pin adds to the moment of the actuating force, so the normal force grows beyond what the actuating force alone would give. If the effect becomes strong enough ($\mu\ge b/c$), the brake locks on by itself.

questions.stem: What happens to the kinetic energy of a vehicle that is brought to rest by its brakes?

options.text: It is converted to heat in the brakes, which then dissipate it to the surroundings
It is stored as potential energy in the brake pads
It is returned to the engine in a conventional braking system

questions.correctOptionText: It is converted to heat in the brakes, which then dissipate it to the surroundings

distractorRationale.a: Correct: friction turns kinetic energy into heat.
distractorRationale.b: Energy is conserved and is not stored in the pads.
distractorRationale.c: Energy is not destroyed; it is transformed.
distractorRationale.d: A conventional friction brake does not return energy.

questions.explanation: Friction does negative work on the rotating parts, and the energy appears as thermal energy in the disc or drum and the lining. The heat is then lost to the air by convection and radiation.

questions.stem: A short-shoe brake has perpendicular distances $b=180$ mm and $c=240$ mm. What minimum coefficient of friction would cause the self-energising shoe to self-lock?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: self-locking when mu c = b, so mu = 180/240 = 0.75.
distractorRationale.c: 0.43 is neither ratio of these distances.
distractorRationale.d: 0.25 is a typical lining value, not the threshold.

questions.explanation: The denominator $b-\mu c$ in $N=Fa/(b-\mu c)$ reaches zero when $\mu=b/c=180/240=0.75$. Beyond that the friction moment alone holds the shoe against the drum, so the brake grabs.

questions.stem: A vehicle's speed doubles from 50 km/h to 100 km/h. By what factor does the kinetic energy that the brakes must absorb change?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: E = (1/2) m v^2 grows with the square of speed.
distractorRationale.b: A doubling would apply if energy were proportional to speed.
distractorRationale.c: Eight times corresponds to a cubic relationship.
distractorRationale.d: The energy depends strongly on speed.

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is $\tfrac12mv^2$, so doubling the speed gives $2^2=4$ times the energy. Braking distance at constant deceleration also rises by a factor of four.

questions.stem: Why is the braking torque of a disc brake less sensitive to changes in the coefficient of friction than that of a self-energising drum brake?

options.text: Disc torque is directly proportional to $\mu$ because there is no friction moment feeding back into the clamping force
Disc brakes are not affected by temperature
Disc brakes use a different friction material
Disc brakes have a larger radius

questions.correctOptionText: Disc torque is directly proportional to $\mu$ because there is no friction moment feeding back into the clamping force

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the clamp force is independent of friction, so $T\propto\mu$.
distractorRationale.b: Disc brakes do suffer fade at high temperature.
distractorRationale.c: Material is not the reason for the difference in sensitivity.
distractorRationale.d: The radius does not change the form of the dependence on mu.

questions.explanation: In a drum shoe $N$ itself depends on $\mu$ through $b-\mu c$, so a small drop in $\mu$ has a magnified effect. In a disc brake the clamp force is set by the hydraulics, so torque simply follows $\mu$.

questions.stem: A rotating machine part has a moment of inertia of 2.0 kg m$^2$ and turns at 3000 rev/min. Find the kinetic energy that the brake must absorb to stop it, in kJ.
questions.explanation: The angular speed is $\omega=2\pi\times3000/60=314.16$ rad/s. The energy is $E=\tfrac12I\omega^2=\tfrac12\times2.0\times314.16^2=98696$ J, which is 98.7 kJ.

questions.stem: A short-shoe brake has a drum radius $r=200$ mm and $\mu=0.35$. An actuating force $F=250$ N acts at perpendicular distance $a=350$ mm from the pin, and the perpendicular distances from the pin to the normal and friction forces are $b=140$ mm and $c=180$ mm. The shoe is in the self-energising direction. Find the braking torque in N m.
questions.explanation: The normal force is $N=Fa/(b-\mu c)=250\times350/(140-0.35\times180)=87500/77=1136$ N. The braking torque is $T=\mu Nr=0.35\times1136\times0.200=79.5$ N m.

questions.stem: A 900 kg car stops from 25 m/s. 60 per cent of the kinetic energy goes to the front axle, which has two discs of mass 6 kg each ($c_p=480$ J/(kg K)). Find the temperature rise of one front disc in K, ignoring cooling.
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy is $\tfrac12\times900\times25^2=281250$ J. Each front disc absorbs $0.6\times281250/2=84375$ J, so $\Delta T=84375/(6\times480)=29.3$ K.

questions.stem: Derive the braking torque of a short-shoe drum brake by taking moments about the pivot, for both directions of drum rotation. Explain what is meant by the self-energising effect and what the condition for self-locking is.
markingGuide: Forces on shoe: actuating force $F$ (arm $a$), normal force $N$ (arm $b$) and friction $\mu N$ (arm $c$), all moments about the pivot.
Self-energising rotation: friction moment helps $F$; $Fa+\mu Nc=Nb$ gives $N=Fa/(b-\mu c)$.
De-energising rotation: $Fa=Nb+\mu Nc$ gives $N=Fa/(b+\mu c)$ and lower torque.
Self-locking when $b-\mu c\le0$, that is $\mu\ge b/c$; the brake then applies itself without actuating force.
Consequence: self-energising increases torque but makes it very sensitive to $\mu$, which is a stability problem.
questions.explanation: Friction changes the moment balance of the shoe, so the normal force depends on $\mu$. This is what creates both the servo effect and the risk of locking.

questions.stem: A designer must estimate whether a disc brake will overheat in an emergency stop. Describe how the energy to be dissipated is determined, how the temperature rise of the disc in a single stop is estimated, what the main assumptions are and why a repeated-stop case needs a different treatment.
markingGuide: Energy from kinetic energy $\tfrac12mv^2$ (and $\tfrac12I\omega^2$ for rotating parts, plus potential energy on a downhill).
Brake force distribution: the share to the front or rear axle and per disc.
Temperature rise $\Delta T=E_d/(m_dc_p)$ with specific heat of the disc material.
Assumptions: all energy goes into the disc, uniform temperature, no heat loss during the stop; hence an upper-bound estimate (in reality the pads absorb some and the surface is hotter than the bulk).

Repeated stops: heat input per stop must be balanced against convection and radiation between stops, so the temperature builds up; needs a thermal model with cooling coefficient and time between stops, and a check for fade and cracking.
questions.explanation: The single-stop estimate treats the disc as a thermal mass. Real discs also lose heat, and in repeated braking the balance between heating and cooling governs.
